speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The Labour Movement acknowledges the need for FTAs in this age of globalisation but we too recognise the need to support our local workforce's aspirations and to address their concerns and anxieties.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The economic disruption brought about by COVID-19 has amplified the fears and anxieties of Professionals, Managers and Executives (PMEs), particularly on the increased competition for jobs and employment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Mature PMEs are especially impacted and vulnerable in this recession.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We will therefore need to take further steps to strengthen the Singaporean Core by levelling the playing field for our Singaporean PMEs and ensuring fairness whether in terms of hiring opportunities and practices in the course of employment or when the employment relationship is terminated.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Co-chairing the NTUC PME task force, we have engaged more than 9,000 the last six months.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I can feel the fears and anxieties of our local PMEs, especially over job security.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Besides ground sentiments on intense competition from the influx of foreign PMEs, I have a compendium of anecdotes of unfair employment practices by employers who favour hiring foreigners and discriminate against our locals.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Just last Thursday, one mature PME who used to be from the financial sector and is now with one of our institutes of higher learning (IHLs) wrote to me an email to share how he witnessed first-hand discriminatory practices at the workplace, resulting in a fellow mature local PME being displaced.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: While the Government had implemented several changes to the foreign manpower policies over the past years, many PMEs feel that the policy tweaks are insufficient to curb unfair competition as there are still companies that continue to engage in unacceptable practices.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Some PMEs view the Fair Consideration Framework (FCF) job advertisement requirement as mere window dressing as employers may already have a foreign candidate in mind when they post their job advertisements.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In addition, many PMEs opined that there is currently no proper framework for the transfer of knowledge for roles which employers claim in which there are skill shortages.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: One of the PMEs shared with me on how he had received a job offer from an IT company with unfair terms and conditions, such as having to pay for damages, including incremental cost of finding replacement and other associated costs like advertisement and consultant fees in the event of his resignation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: He believed that this is an underhand tactic by the company to eventually inform the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) that they had offered the job to Singaporeans but none accepted it so that they are able to hire an Employment Pass (EP) holder.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am heartened that in my past 10 years of lobbying and advocating for a stronger Singaporean Core that many measures have been put in place to support and protect our Singaporean PMEs and provide them with a fair and level playing field in the job market.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: That said, more needs to be done to strengthen the Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We must further develop our local workforce's capabilities and protect our locals from being unfairly discriminated against.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Our local PMEs are unhappy when many of the roles which they can undertake and do are instead taken up by foreign PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is important to recognise the role that foreign manpower plays, which is to complement and enhance the capabilities of the local workforce and not to replace it.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: First, we can enhance fair hiring practices through: one, improving our HR standards and practices to ensure that companies are equipped with adequate knowledge of employment legislation and regulations to improve compliance with fair employment practices; and two, strengthening enforcement and imposing stiffer penalties for errant companies with discriminatory hiring practices.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This will then send a clear message against workplace discrimination and eradicate unfair hiring practices, whether it is with respect to age, gender, marital status, nationality, disability, race, religion or sexual orientation and so on.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The point system will then be used to evaluate and approve the EP application.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We must ensure concerted, structured, institutionalised and mandatory skills and knowledge transfer from these foreign PMEs to our local PMEs within a stipulated and agreed time frame in the spirit of complementarity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: (In Mandarin):   Faced with the triple challenges posed by industry transformation, digitalisation and COVID-19, our PMEs are worried about employment and job competition.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I urge that we strengthen relevant measures, policies and legislations to build a workforce with a Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: (In English): Mdm Deputy Speaker, the Labour Movement has consistently advocated for a stronger Singaporean Core and will continue to champion for our workers' interests to ensure that there must be fairness and zero tolerance for discrimination of any kind.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is ever more critical for us to ensure that Singaporeans are considered and treated fairly, especially in the current economic and employment climate.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the same vein, we will continue to collaborate with our tripartite partners to nurture and develop our workers through training and skills transfer so that they will benefit from better careers and development opportunities in a progressive work environment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In my speech, I will talk about three types of discrimination that are commonly complained about in the workplace: racial discrimination, ageism and preferential bias for foreign employees over local employees.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Similar to my 2019 Adjournment Motion, I want to again propose enhancing anti-discrimination laws, localising the workforce through targets and according more resources and powers to the TAFEP.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Malay):   These days, Singaporeans feel more encouraged to speak up on social media about racial discrimination.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Among these allegations, many are of malpractices in our workplaces, where the race of an employee is used as a conduit to gain unjust preference against others.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This was a slight increase from the 58.7% of Malays and 52.6% of Indians who said this five years ago.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These incidences suggest that racism and stereotyping persist in our workplace.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Victims are unaware or perhaps doubt the effectiveness of official channels to seek help, so they post it on social media instead.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Resultantly, it appears or is perceived on the ground as the authorities' approach to discrimination being more reactive than proactive, which is not a true reflection of the efforts of TAFEP and MOM.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In English): While our younger Singaporeans can turn to social media to vent about their unpleasant experiences with racism and prejudice, it is different for our older employees who have faced similar discrimination at their age.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some are simply not active social media users or are not comfortable with the potential attention from netizens and they are suffering in silence.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The rate of age discrimination in the Singaporean workforce is higher than the average of 12% in the Asia Pacific region.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We also have locals feeling that they are being discriminated against when applying to a company with many foreign management staff.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They believe that foreigners in a hiring position are more inclined to hire and promote people of their own nationality.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some may argue that these are mere general statistics.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But I have seen residents coming to me for help for alleged discriminatory practices by employers in these areas above.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must be more assertive against discrimination of any kind.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The UK, for example, has very comprehensive and explicit laws to tackle hiring discrimination and it covers from gender, race, age, marriage, maternity, to disability.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Equality Act 2010 legally protects people from discrimination in the workplace and in wider society.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It replaced previous anti-discrimination laws with a single Act, making the law easier to understand and strengthening protection in some situations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It sets out different ways in which it is unlawful to treat someone.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Act also specifically puts the onus on employers to produce justification for setting age criteria for their employment process.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Currently, our equality laws are ambiguous and some employers take advantage of loopholes or feign ignorance.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, on addressing the prejudice experienced by Singaporeans in companies with a large population of foreign employees, I would suggest legislation to include that all foreign management staff in hiring positions should be made to undergo compulsory training on employment and hiring practices in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is so that there are no excuses for anyone to claim ignorance of our commitment to non-discriminatory work practices.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, I would ask for concrete targets to localise our workforce.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hiring foreigners to fill skill gaps is a necessity, but allowing this to continue with no effort to localise after an extended period of time, is simply not reflective of good corporate citizenship.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our localisation efforts can be targeted for a range of skills and companies can incorporate elements of training for eventual local employment and with a specific localisation target, for example, in three to five years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The HR departments of companies would be a good place to start as they handle recruitment, training and welfare of employees.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As part of the localisation strategies, I would like to reiterate my proposal to expand the Capability Transfer Programme (CTP) to support the transfer of capabilities from foreign employees currently employed in Singapore to local employees.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I would go as far as to suggest TAFEP and MOM form a dedicated enforcement unit to focus efforts on helping companies to localise and to identify and penalise recalcitrant offenders that are guilty of poor corporate citizenship.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A single brand for both enforcement and developmental efforts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some employers are so intoxicated by their discriminatory practices that they are inured to the penalties.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need to go beyond issuing them fines or temporarily suspending work passes which perhaps to them is a minor inconvenience in the grand scheme of things that matter to them.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: TAFEP is here to act and I believe so too MOM.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, let us not hesitate to act with more punch against errant employers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Unions may consider embedding this in their Collective Agreements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Today, I will speak about the unfair discrimination women and mothers face before they take even a single step in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am speaking up about this again because it is clear that women are treated unfairly at the workplaces.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our female labour force participation rate also shows a disparity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The most recent quarter of data shows that women’s labour participation rate was 61.2%, far below the 75.4% for men.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Last year, a female resident shared worrying concerns with me.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She said, "I have just been to an interview.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The HR personnel called me a mother before they even called me by my name.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am in the line of recruitment and such stories are a dime a dozen.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My take is that the focus should be on whether we are up for the job.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It should not be on whether we are a mother and then assume that we are not able to do the role."  I have personally witnessed the conditions my resident talked about.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At one job fair that I visited just this past year, I was encouraged by the efforts to help locals find new jobs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What was less encouraging to see was that almost every single booth that I visited asked in their application forms about the marital status and number of children of the applicants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These questions have nothing to do with how capable an applicant is and they disproportionately hurt the chances of women and mothers to find employment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A study by researchers at Cornell University found that women who did not have children were two times more likely to be called for an interview, as compared with similarly qualified mothers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Questions about marital status, number of children and plans to have children are not one-off.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They are widespread in our economy and a standard part of many companies’ recruitment processes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Last year, I launched a public survey about this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Fifty percent were asked whether they have had or planned to have children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: More than 60% felt that having children or planning to have children would make them more likely to be rejected or to be offered a lower salary.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One respondent said, "At a final interview with a local bank, they blatantly told me that I should not get pregnant if I were to take on the role."  Over the weekend, just this weekend, another young mother shared with me about the numerous times she faced discrimination during job interviews.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She was asked about her childcare arrangements, who would pick up and drop off the child and even whether she would not do work when her child is unwell.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She shared with me, “My husband has never once been subjected to questions similar to those which I have received at interviews or ever been "grilled" about our childcare arrangement; or whether he is sure he can put in the work required even when his interviewers are aware that he is married and has a child”.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The young mother asked me, “Is it fair that they get penalised for it before even being given the opportunity to prove their worth?” Indeed, questions about marital status and number of children are harmful.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They hurt the job prospects of all women, with mothers particularly suffering.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They hurt employers as they may miss out finding the best candidate for their roles.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They hurt our nation’s standing as a society that provides fair opportunities to women.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Fortunately, we do not have to start from scratch in tackling such discrimination.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have the Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practice, or the Tripartite Guidelines for short.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Tripartite Guidelines on job application forms prohibit questions on age, gender, race, religion, marital status, family responsibilities and disability.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Guidelines are a step in the right direction by setting out fair and responsible employment and hiring practices.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, the Tripartite Guidelines remain that – guidelines.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the meantime, questions that clearly flout the guidelines are openly asked on application forms and in job interviews.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The reality is that these Guidelines are a weak deterrence and are routinely flouted.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The current penalty of curtailing work pass privileges for non-compliance is neither appropriate nor sufficient.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is inappropriate because it makes no sense.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are telling companies that treating women with fairness is important if you want to hire foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is insufficient because it does not cover every employer.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If you do not hire foreign workers, how would you be hurt by curtailment of work pass privileges?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I know I usually ask for many things.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It would address not only discrimination on the basis of gender or marital status, but also protects against workplace discrimination based on age, race, religion and disability.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It would also provide more methods for enforcement and a wider range of penalties to tackle workplace discrimination.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If we are serious about tackling discrimination, we should not tie our own hands by wielding only the blunt tool of work pass privileges.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We know that MOM is the most compassionate Ministry and I hope MOM will say yes to us.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They have been championing these issues for many years, together with other People’s Action Party (PAP) and Labour Members of Parliament, both past and present.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These issues are indeed top of mind and longstanding priorities for MOM too.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will address them in two ways today: one, enabling Singaporeans to succeed as industries and jobs transform; and two, tackling workplace discrimination.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I will speak on our key efforts in these areas and plans to strengthen fair employment standards.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: By accelerating technology adoption and equipping Singaporeans with skillsets for future jobs, we will enable them to seize new opportunities and succeed at the workplace.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Businesses will also have a strong local talent pool to support their transformation efforts and growth to compete globally.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is a win-win for all of us.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Jobs and skills for Singaporeans are at the front and centre of MOM’s as well as sector agencies’ plans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The 23 Industry Transformation Maps guide our efforts to upskill and reskill Singaporeans at various stages of their careers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our graduates are equipped with industry know-how at our Institutes of Higher Learning and we support lifelong learning and skills mastery through the national SkillsFuture movement.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Middle-age workers making mid-career switches are supported through Career Conversion Programmes or CCPs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Today, there are over 100 CCPs across 30 sectors and more are being added every year.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our close partnership with employers, with industry associations ensure that training is always relevant to employers' needs and this means our workers see direct benefits.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Programmes such as the Technology in Finance Immersion and TechSkills Accelerator help Singaporeans gain exposure and experience in key tech areas in the financial services sector and allow company-led training programmes to accelerate professional development in 5G, Internet of Things and cybersecurity respectively.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOM is also working with sector agencies to develop Jobs Transformation Maps (JTMs) with detailed job-level insights on the impact of technology on each industry.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have already launched three JTMs: one for HR, one for logistics and another one for the financial services sector.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These JTMs will be a useful compass to prepare all of our workers for the future of work.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To encourage local hiring, we introduced the Jobs Growth Incentive (JGI) in September 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In fact, our efforts to support our local workforce in tackling accelerated structural changes have been commended by the International Monetary Fund.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The work is, of course, never finished and we will continue to press on.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I can understand the anxieties that Singaporeans feel in an open and competitive labour market.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But I assure you that MOM deals with workplace discrimination with utmost seriousness.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will ensure that Singaporeans are considered fairly for employment opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In my Ministerial Statement on 6 July, I elaborated extensively on how our work pass framework ensures that Singaporeans have fair access to jobs in a very dynamic labour market.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: However, I want to also reiterate the importance of staying and remaining open.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The combination of skilled locals and a diversity of foreign expertise is a key competitive advantage for us in drawing many international companies here, creating more good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Beyond nationality-based discrimination, we will and we must also tackle other types of discrimination as well, including on grounds of sex, age, religion, race and disabilities and this must happen across all phases of employment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In fact, MOM has been working on this for more than two decades, progressively stepping up our efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We started with the Tripartite Guidelines on Non-Discriminatory Job Advertisements in 1999 and we formed the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices in 2006.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We launched the Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practices (TGFEP) in 2007, which clearly outlines the principles and the practices which employers must adopt at different stages of employment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Since 2013, we have penalised employers who do not abide by the TGFEP by suspending their work pass privileges.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Fair Consideration Framework (FCF) was also introduced to set clear expectations of employers to consider the workforce in Singapore fairly.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: More recently, we have also stiffened penalties for all forms of workplace discrimination.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The current approach has worked well for us thus far.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Employment outcomes for groups such as women and seniors have improved.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And they are, in fact, better than in some advanced economies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If we look at the employment rate of women aged 25 to 64, it has risen steadily from about 66% in 2010 to 73% in 2020, holding steady amidst the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our adjusted Gender Pay Gap is also lower than in some advanced economies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: TAFEP's experience has also been that most employers are cooperative in working with them to close HR gaps.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In recent years, several Members have raised the possibility of legislation to give more enforcement bite to the TGFEP and the Fair Consideration Framework (FCF).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We received similar feedback through the Conversations on Singapore Women's Development.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have never been closed to such suggestions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: However, laws alone do not guarantee better employment outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We must weigh the costs and benefits and we must determine what would work best in Singapore's interest and in the Singaporean context.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, on the one hand, legislation will provide a clear premise to publicise the names of companies found to have breached the law, but on the other hand, we should also be mindful of the unintended consequences.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Committee should be able to arrive at a decision on the approach that is in the best interests of workers and Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Like many Members in this House, we want to build on the progress we have made.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We want to work towards fairer and more progressive workplaces, while preserving our competitiveness.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is not a panacea and it is not a silver bullet.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We need a balanced suite of measures and to not be hampered by an overly rigid framework that hurts all parties involved.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Only then can we continue to give Singaporeans the best chance to get ahead and to secure their livelihoods.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: The time allowed for the proceedings has expired.
